title: East Africa and Britain
hookLine: many Sikh families moved from Kenya and Uganda to Britain

cards: Two journeys, one suitcase. It sits battered in a loft in an English town, with two faded labels on its side: one from Nairobi or Kampala, one from London.

Inside, wrapped in cloth, are a few photographs of a house with a tin roof and a garden of mango trees, and a gutka, a small book of daily prayers, its corners soft from use. A grandmother keeps it there.
Her own parents had left Punjab for East Africa. Then she left East Africa for Britain. Today is about families who moved twice.

teach.b: In British times, community histories say, Sikhs from Punjab went to Kenya and Uganda as craftsmen, builders and railway workers, and then as shopkeepers, teachers and civil servants.
They built gurdwaras there, and children grew up who had never seen Punjab. Second, the second move.

In the years after Kenya and Uganda became independent, life grew uncertain for Asian families, and in Uganda they were ordered to leave. Many Sikh families came to Britain with what they could carry.
Some arrived with skills, savings or English; some arrived with very little. Third, the arrival.

In towns across Britain, these families helped found and grow gurdwaras, often in old buildings bought together and made over by hand. They had done this once already, in Africa, so they knew how. Fourth, the old story.

In the janamsakhis, the traditional tales of Guru Nanak, the Guru visits two villages. One treats him rudely, and he blesses it to stay where it is. The other welcomes him warmly, and he blesses it to be scattered.
His companion is puzzled, and the Guru explains: let the good people scatter, so that goodness spreads wherever they go.
Families who moved twice sometimes tell that story with a smile. Being scattered was hard. It was also, in that old tale, a kind of blessing.

how: Sikh families of East African background are part of the sangat in British gurdwaras, and some congregations were founded or grown by them.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak. one village was rude to you, one welcomed you. what blessing do you give the welcoming one?
games.why: in the janamsakhi tale, he blesses the good village to scatter, so goodness spreads wherever its people go.

practice: Think of someone you know who has had to start again more than once, a grandparent, a neighbor, a friend from school, maybe you, and picture the boxes, the new street, the first winter.
Breathe in and honor what it cost; breathe out and honor what they built anyway. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for those still unpacking; if you don't, just hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Pardes. A foreign land far from home: Kenya and Uganda, then Britain, where Sikh families who left Punjab twice built gurdwaras both times. Today's word.
